Well, we use what facilities we have at hand. The hon. gentleman might be surprised to know that the commercial incubator used in the spring hatching season is used to dry a good deal of corn.
So far as the marketing of com is concerned, in the particular area from which my hon. friend comes, the production is local though it may be extended to other sections; but I presume that there is much localized production of seed and grain com as well. Experience in many places in the west has shown that where such communities are specializing in a certain type of crop it is not so difficult to organize some sort of marketing concern among them. I refer particularly to the alfalfa growers of southern Alberta and another group of alfalfa growers in northern Manitoba who have specialized extensively in the production of alfalfa seed. These organizations, through their very careful selection of seed and their careful cleaning of it, have established a reputation, and as a cooperative organization have joined together in the matter of sales with the result that they have gone along very well.
While listening to other hon. members discussing this question it occurred to me that in some of the statutes that have already been

passed some assistance might be given to the corn growers in connection with drying. I know that a subvention is provided for between the dominion government and the government of the province for the purpose of establishing seed-cleaning plants in different parts of the country. In our province there are a number of them. There is one not far from where I live where brome-grass-growing is specialized in. There the two governments cooperated in equipping that organization with a splendid seed-cleaning plant. If that is necessary for seed-cleaning probably it is equally necessary for drying com, and something might be done to assist the corn growers in that regard.
I wish my hon. friend the very best of luck in the consideration which will be given by the government to his resolution. I have nothing against the resolution, but hon. members, particularly those on the agriculture committee, are interested in the matter, and I imagine if he would press it there would be no difficulty in having the agriculture committee meet on one or two occasions to deal with the matter, merely for the purpose of securing additional information, calling before it departmental officials and others interested, probably including some from his own district. I offer that suggestion to him.
Reference was made by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle to the tariff on corn imposed by the former government. At that time I stated that I did not see what difference it made to put a duty on com. The idea they were propounding then was that by placing a duty on corn they could increase the consumption of barley, which at that time was a drug on the market. My observation was to the effect that I could not see what difference it made whether our barley was competing with com in a foreign market or com was competing with our barley in this market.
As the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Euler) may wish to make a few remarks on the resolution, I shall make way for him.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. D. EULER (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
maintopic: PROPOSED IMPROVED MARKETING FACILITIES AND PROVISION FOR STORAGE, DRYING, GRADING AND INSPECTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as a matter of fact I have no extended comments to make on the resolution. In the few minutes at my disposal I might take the opportunity to compliment the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) not only on the mass of valuable information he has placed before the house, but also on the manner in which he did this. I was particularly interested when he said that the corn grown in the western Ontario peninsula is of as good quality as corn grown anywhere else in the world. I admit that while I have no intimate knowledge of the

Com-Marketing and Storage
corn question, the information I had rather led me to believe that because of the greater moisture content of Canadian com it was under somewhat of a disability as compared with corn produced elsewhere. But if it is true that in western Ontario or anywhere else in Canada we can grow com which is as good as that from any other country in the world, surely it is an anomaly that we cannot at least supply our own Canadian market.
This matter of the production, grading, drying and storage of com to some extent comes under the care of two departments, the Department of Agriculture and the Department of Trade and Commerce. I need not say to my hon. friends, especially those across the. way, that these two departments cooperate in everything in the highest degree-

maintopic: PROPOSED IMPROVED MARKETING FACILITIES AND PROVISION FOR STORAGE, DRYING, GRADING AND INSPECTION

-and they are quite willing to do so with regard to the production and sale of corn. The factors in the situation which have been discussed most particularly seem to be marketing, storage, drying, grading and inspection. All of these affect the quality of the commodity. I am glad to know that inherently the quality of Canadian com is what my hon. friend says it is. The question of quality has not been brought particularly to the attention of the Department of Trade and Commerce. I cannot recall that the matter of grading and inspection was ever brought before the department. I know that the question of storage was brought before the Department of Trade and Commerce in the time of the former government, and also of the present government. That particular matter is not being stressed to-day, and I might leave it with this statement, that there is not wanting in Canada at the moment equipment for either storage or drying of com. I regret that my colleague the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) is not here to-day, because many of the matters under discussion come more particularly within his province.
I -might summarize the results of some investigations made by members of the Department of Agriculture and the Department of Trade and Commerce: There is much poor quality com, resulting from admixture of varieties, too many varieties and poor varieties; also poor culture and harvesting practices, and lack of suitable com cribs on the farm. This is not entirely consistent with the statements which have been -made that Canadian corn is just as good in quality as other corn, but this is easily capable of correction. Then there is the matter which has been mentioned, that much of the corn has too high a moisture content, which causes heating in storage after shipping and is therefore a 51952-894
serious drawback. There are insufficient hogs in the corn area to consume at a profit the inferior com and keep it off the market. There is also still a good deal of damage caused by the corn-borer. Finally-and this touches the Department of Trade and Commerce-the official grades and inspection services for both seed and commercial com are inadequate. As far as the seed com is concerned, I think that is entirely a matter for the Department of Agriculture, but grading and inspection are for the Department of Trade and Commerce, through the grain board, which is under the jurisdiction of that department.
Now my time is up. In conclusion I should like to say that as far as the matters discussed to-day affect the Department of Agriculture, I am sure my colleague the Minister of Agriculture will take due note of what has been said. I shall further bring it to his attention. With regard to the matter of inspection and grading, in 1936 the Department of Agriculture reported that an adequate system of inspection and grading of commercial corn was vital to any successful development of market practice, and recommended that the whole question of commercial grades of com should be reviewed. It has been brought before the board of grain commissioners, and they reported that the machinery for inspection and grading was inadequate, contrary to the expression of opinion by the hon. member who preceded me (Mr. Weir). Section 36 of the Canada Grain Act provides:
No inspecting officer in the eastern division shall be required to inspect any grain which is not in the district to which such officer has been assigned, or to inspect any grain in such district more than five miles from his office unless the person requesting such inspection has first paid to the inspecting officer a sum sufficient to cover such officer's travelling expenses between his office and the place where such grain is and return, and also such an allowance for his time as the board may direct.
There is only one grain inspector for Ontario, and he is located in Toronto. But as a result of consultation between the Department of Agriculture and the board of grain commissioners, it was arranged:
1.	That the Department of Agriculture would consider the present definitions of the different grades of corn, and suggest to the Board of Grain Commissioners any changes which they might feel were necessary.
2.	That the Board of Grain Commissioners as an experiment would provide for the local inspection of corn in Ontario under the Canada Grain Act, and that officials of the Department of Agriculture would, as far as possible, carry on inspection services under the direction of the board's chief grain inspector, all actual details of the procedure to be worked out later,
Privilege-Mr. Pelletier

after discussion between the Board of Grain Commissioners' chief grain inspector and officials of the Department of Agriculture.
When the general revision of the Canada Grain Act is undertaken, we hope such amendments will be made as will meet the wishes of those who have spoken here this afternoon. In the meantime, Mr. Speaker, I have no objection to the carrying of the resolution.
Motion (Mr. Martin) agreed to.
